domains.title: Absolute Divine Identity And Scriptural Monotheism
domains.anchor: Deuteronomy 6:4 — "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD."

scripture.excerpt: The LORD our God is one LORD.
scripture.function: The Shema — the irreducible creed of biblical monotheism; every subsequent doctrine interprets within it.

scripture.excerpt: Before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me.
scripture.function: God denies the existence of any prior or subsequent deity — absolute and exclusive divine identity.

scripture.excerpt: I am the first, and I am the last; and beside me there is no God.
scripture.function: Eternity of identity with absolute exclusivity — no God alongside or within a Godhead of persons.

scripture.excerpt: I am the LORD, and there is none else, there is no God beside me.
scripture.function: The strongest possible monotheistic declaration — no qualification, no plurality.

scripture.excerpt: The LORD our God is one LORD.
scripture.function: Jesus affirms the Shema as the greatest commandment — he is not offering a trinitarian revision.

scripture.excerpt: There is none other God but one... one God, the Father.
scripture.function: Paul's apostolic monotheism is absolute — not a generic theism but specifically covenantal oneness.

scripture.excerpt: One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all.
scripture.function: Seven unities — each "one" is absolute, not relational or economic.

scripture.excerpt: For there is one God, and one mediator... the man Christ Jesus.
scripture.function: The unity of God and the humanity of Christ affirmed in the same breath — no separate divine persons.

vocabulary.definition: The belief in one and only one God as opposed to polytheism or any form of plurality within deity.
vocabulary.relevance: The doctrinal category that defines the entire domain — all standards interpret within it.

vocabulary.definition: Hebrew: "Shema Yisrael Adonai Eloheinu Adonai Echad" (Deut. 6:4) — Israel's foundational confession of divine unity.
vocabulary.relevance: The anchor text of the domain; every claim about God's oneness is measured against it.

vocabulary.definition: Hebrew word meaning "one" used in the Shema — denotes absolute unity, not compound unity.
vocabulary.relevance: Critical for refuting the trinitarian claim that "one" in the OT means a "compound one."

vocabulary.definition: One in number — as opposed to "oneness" meaning unity of will or purpose among multiple persons.
vocabulary.relevance: Distinguishes the Oneness position from trinitarianism at the most foundational level.

vocabulary.definition: The biblical claim that God alone exists as
vocabulary.relevance: Grounded in Isaiah's declarations; refutes

vocabulary.definition: The attempt to define God through Greek philosophical categories (substance, person, essence) rather than Scripture.
vocabulary.relevance: Identifies the historical pressure that distorted biblical monotheism in the 2nd– 4th centuries.

domains.title: The Nature And Attributes Of The One God
domains.anchor: John 4:24 — "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth."

scripture.excerpt: God is a Spirit.
scripture.function: Defines God's essential nature — immaterial, non-physical, unlimited — prior to all discussion of persons or roles.

scripture.excerpt: Ye saw no manner of similitude... take ye therefore good heed unto yourselves.
scripture.function: Israel saw no form at Sinai — God's invisible nature is foundational, not incidental.

scripture.excerpt: From everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.
scripture.function: God's eternal self-existence — he has no beginning and no dependence on anything outside himself.

scripture.excerpt: I am the LORD, I change not.
scripture.function: Divine immutability — God's nature, character, and purposes are absolutely stable.

scripture.excerpt: His understanding is unsearchable.
scripture.function: Divine omniscience and transcendence — God's knowledge has no limits and no external source.

scripture.excerpt: Do not I fill heaven and earth?
scripture.function: Omnipresence — God's presence is not localized or bounded.

scripture.excerpt: The Lord God omnipotent reigneth.
scripture.function: Omnipotence — absolute sovereignty over all created things.

scripture.excerpt: The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious...
scripture.function: God's moral attributes as he declares them to Moses — the fullest OT self-declaration.

vocabulary.definition: Divine attributes that God alone possesses and cannot share with creatures — omniscience, omnipotence, omnipresence, aseity, immutability.
vocabulary.relevance: Grounds the absolute distinction between Creator and creation.

vocabulary.definition: Divine attributes that God shares in limited measure with humans — love, justice, holiness, mercy, truth.
vocabulary.relevance: Grounded in the image of God (Gen. 1:26– 27); the basis for human moral obligation.

vocabulary.definition: God's absolute self-existence — he exists from and by himself, dependent on nothing.
vocabulary.relevance: Distinguishes the biblical God from philosophical first principles or forces.

vocabulary.definition: God does not change in his nature, character, or eternal purposes.
vocabulary.relevance: Critical for distinguishing the eternal Word from the incarnational Son — the divine nature did not change at the incarnation.

vocabulary.definition: God is fully present everywhere simultaneously — not distributed or
vocabulary.relevance: Provides the ground for the Holy Spirit's universal operation and the indwelling of

vocabulary.definition: God's absolute moral purity and total otherness from sin and all that is creaturely.
vocabulary.relevance: The foundational moral attribute — all other moral attributes flow from it.

domains.title: God Revealed In Creation, Covenant, And Judgment
domains.anchor: Genesis 1:1 — "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth."

scripture.excerpt: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
scripture.function: God as sole Creator — not an emanation, committee, or agent, but the one divine Person acting alone.

scripture.excerpt: Let us make man in our image.
scripture.function: The plural of deliberation (royal/majestic) or address to the heavenly court — not a proof of trinity; the singular "image" (v.27) confirms one Creator.

scripture.excerpt: All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made.
scripture.function: Identifies Jesus (the Word) as the Creator — same Creator as Genesis 1, not a second divine agent.

scripture.excerpt: For by him were all things created... all things were created by him and for him.
scripture.function: Paul's unambiguous statement that Jesus is the Creator of all things — fully identified with the God of Genesis 1.

scripture.excerpt: I will put enmity between thee and the woman...
scripture.function: The protoevangelion — the first covenant promise of a Redeemer, embedded in the judgment of the fall.

scripture.excerpt: The token of the covenant... a bow in the cloud.
scripture.function: God's covenantal commitment to creation — sovereignty expressed through binding promise.

scripture.excerpt: Shall there be evil in a city, and the LORD hath not done it?
scripture.function: Divine judgment is not passive — God is the active Lord of history, including its darkest episodes.

scripture.excerpt: The heavens declare the glory of God.
scripture.function: Creation's testimony to its Creator — general revelation as the first witness to divine glory.

vocabulary.definition: Creation from nothing — God created not from pre-existing matter but by his sovereign word alone.
vocabulary.relevance: Establishes God's absolute sovereignty as Creator and the contingency of all that exists.

vocabulary.definition: The "first gospel" — Genesis 3:15, where God promises a redeemer even in the judgment of the fall.
vocabulary.relevance: Shows that redemption is embedded in creation theology from the beginning.

vocabulary.definition: A binding agreement initiated by God that defines the relationship between God and his people, typically including promises, obligations, and a sign.
vocabulary.relevance: The structural category through which God's relationship with humanity is organized throughout Scripture.

vocabulary.definition: God's self-disclosure through creation, conscience, and history — available to all
vocabulary.relevance: Establishes human moral accountability even without the written Word (Rom.

vocabulary.definition: God's direct, verbal, and redemptive self- disclosure — primarily through Scripture and ultimately in Jesus Christ.
vocabulary.relevance: The primary category of doctrinal knowledge; creation's witness leads to, but cannot replace, scriptural revelation.

vocabulary.definition: God's ongoing governance of all creation — sustaining, directing, and bringing his purposes to completion.
vocabulary.relevance: Connects the God of creation to the God of redemption as one continuous sovereign will.

domains.title: Sinai, The Tabernacle, And The Presence Of God
domains.anchor: Exodus 33:14 — "My presence shall go with thee, and I will give thee rest."

scripture.excerpt: I AM THAT I AM... I AM hath sent me unto you.
scripture.function: God's self-declaration of eternal self- existence at the burning bush — the ground of all covenant identity.

scripture.excerpt: A kingdom of priests, an holy nation.
scripture.function: The Sinai covenant establishes Israel's purpose — to be God's people among the nations.

scripture.excerpt: Let them make me a sanctuary; that I may dwell among them.
scripture.function: God's stated purpose for the tabernacle — divine presence structured for human participation.

scripture.excerpt: A cloud covered the tent of the congregation, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle.
scripture.function: The shekinah glory as the sign of divine presence — the culmination of the tabernacle narrative.

scripture.excerpt: The LORD said unto Moses, Speak unto Aaron thy brother, that he come not at all times into the holy place within the vail.
scripture.function: The separation between God's presence and sinful humanity — bridged only by atonement.

scripture.excerpt: The cloud filled the house of the LORD... the glory of the LORD had filled the house.
scripture.function: The same glory in Solomon's temple — continuity of God's presence through covenant institutions.

scripture.excerpt: The glory of the LORD departed from off the threshold of the house.
scripture.function: The departure of the glory as judgment — God's presence is not unconditional.

scripture.excerpt: The Word was made flesh, and dwelt (tabernacled) among us, and we beheld his glory.
scripture.function: The incarnation as the ultimate tabernacle — God's presence permanently structured in human flesh.

vocabulary.definition: A visible or perceptible manifestation of God to human beings — burning bush, pillar of fire, glory cloud.
vocabulary.relevance: Distinguishes temporary divine appearances from the permanent incarnational presence.

vocabulary.definition: The visible glory or presence of God dwelling among Israel — not a biblical word but a later rabbinic term for the divine luminescence associated with the tabernacle and temple.
vocabulary.relevance: Identifies the phenomenon of God's localized presence as a covenantal reality.

vocabulary.definition: The portable worship structure constructed at Sinai as the dwelling place of God's presence among Israel in the wilderness.
vocabulary.relevance: The architectural type of God's indwelling — fulfilled in the incarnation (John 1:14) and the church (1 Cor. 3:16).

vocabulary.definition: The innermost chamber of the tabernacle/temple containing the ark of
vocabulary.relevance: Represents the inaccessibility of God's presence to sinful humanity — resolved by

vocabulary.definition: A type is an OT person, event, or institution that prefigures its NT fulfillment (the antitype). E.g., the tabernacle (type) → the incarnate Christ and indwelt believer (antitype).
vocabulary.relevance: Provides the interpretive framework for reading OT covenant structures as pointing to Christ.

vocabulary.definition: The permanent residence of the Holy Spirit within a believer — the new covenant fulfillment of the tabernacle's function.
vocabulary.relevance: Connects the OT presence theology to the NT doctrine of the Spirit and new birth.

domains.title: The Names And Titles Of God
domains.anchor: Proverbs 30:4 — "What is his name, and what is his son's name, if thou canst tell?"

scripture.excerpt: The LORD God of your fathers... this is my name for ever.
scripture.function: YHWH as the covenant name of God — permanent, memorial, generational.

scripture.excerpt: His name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.
scripture.function: The Messiah is identified with three divine names: Mighty God, Everlasting Father — not mere titles of honor.

scripture.excerpt: Whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD shall be delivered.
scripture.function: YHWH's name as the means of salvation — applied to Jesus in Acts 2:21 and Romans 10:13.

scripture.excerpt: Thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.
scripture.function: The name Jesus (Yeshua = YHWH saves) encodes the covenant name and the redemptive purpose.

scripture.excerpt: I have manifested thy name unto the men which thou gavest me.
scripture.function: Jesus declares that he has disclosed the Father's name — he is the name-bearer.

scripture.excerpt: Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
scripture.function: The exclusive salvific function of the name of Jesus.

scripture.excerpt: God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name... that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord.
scripture.function: The exaltation of the name of Jesus to universal supremacy — including the YHWH-title "Lord."

scripture.excerpt: His name is called The Word of God.
scripture.function: The glorified Christ bears the title Word — his name encompasses eternity.

vocabulary.definition: The personal covenant name of God in the OT — from the Hebrew root "to be," meaning the self-existent, eternal One.
vocabulary.relevance: The name that carries the full weight of OT monotheism; applied to Jesus in NT texts (e.g., Phil. 2:10–11; Isa. 45:23).

vocabulary.definition: Hebrew title meaning "Lord" or "Master" — used in speech when YHWH appears in the written text, out of reverence.
vocabulary.relevance: The LXX translates YHWH as Kyrios (Lord) — the same word used for Jesus throughout the NT.

vocabulary.definition: The generic Hebrew term for God — El (singular), Elohim (plural of majesty).
vocabulary.relevance: The plurality of Elohim is a grammatical feature (plural of majesty), not a proof of trinitarian persons; used with singular verbs throughout Genesis 1.

vocabulary.definition: God Almighty — the name revealed to Abraham and the patriarchs (Exod. 6:3).
vocabulary.relevance: The covenant name through which God initiated the Abrahamic promises.

vocabulary.definition: Greek term for Lord — the LXX translation
vocabulary.relevance: Establishes the identification of Jesus with

vocabulary.definition: The incarnational name — Yeshua (Hebrew: YHWH saves) rendered into Greek as Iesous, English as Jesus.
vocabulary.relevance: The name that contains both the covenant name (YHWH) and the salvific purpose (saves) — the definitive new covenant name of God.

domains.title: Progressive Revelation And The Prophetic Line
domains.anchor: Hebrews 1:1–2 — "God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son."

scripture.excerpt: God... spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son.
scripture.function: The definitive statement of progressive revelation — prior revelation was genuine but partial; Jesus is the final and fullest word.

scripture.excerpt: I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy.
scripture.function: The prophecy of the Spirit's universal outpouring — a new revelatory age that Acts 2 declares inaugurated.

scripture.excerpt: He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.
scripture.function: The suffering servant prophecy — the fullest OT portrait of the Messiah's atoning work; the church's primary evangelistic OT text.

scripture.excerpt: I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel... I will put my law in their inward parts.
scripture.function: The promise of the new covenant — internalized law, universal knowledge of God, forgiveness.

scripture.excerpt: A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you.
scripture.function: The Spirit's indwelling as the mechanism of new covenant transformation — connects to new birth.

scripture.excerpt: Out of thee shall he come forth... whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.
scripture.function: The Messiah's eternal origin combined with his localized birth — a paradox resolved only by the incarnation.

scripture.excerpt: The Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple.
scripture.function: God himself coming to his temple — applied to Jesus's entry into Jerusalem and the Temple.

scripture.excerpt: All the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen.
scripture.function: Jesus as the fulfillment point of every prophetic promise — progressive revelation finds its terminus in him.

vocabulary.definition: The theological principle that God disclosed himself increasingly over time, with each stage building on and going beyond the previous, culminating in Jesus Christ.
vocabulary.relevance: Explains why OT revelation is genuine but incomplete — and why Jesus is the final word.

vocabulary.definition: The interpretive method of reading OT persons, events, and institutions as anticipatory patterns fulfilled in the NT — especially in Christ.
vocabulary.relevance: Provides the hermeneutical bridge between the two Testaments.

vocabulary.definition: The actualization in history of what the
vocabulary.relevance: Demonstrates the divine authorship of

vocabulary.definition: The theological concept that the "last days" began with the resurrection and Pentecost — the end has already begun, though not yet completed.
vocabulary.relevance: Explains why Peter quotes Joel 2 in Acts 2 — the age of fulfillment has arrived.

vocabulary.definition: Latin: "fuller meaning" — the principle that OT prophecies may carry a richer divine meaning than the human author consciously intended, fully revealed only in NT fulfillment.
vocabulary.relevance: Helps students understand how Isaiah 53 can be more fully about Jesus than Isaiah himself may have understood.

vocabulary.definition: The collection of authoritative books that constitute Scripture — the finished record of God's progressive revelation.
vocabulary.relevance: Grounds the concept of a closed, sufficient revelation — progressive revelation is now complete in Jesus and the apostolic witness.

domains.title: Jesus Christ As The Full Revelation Of God
domains.anchor: Colossians 2:9 — "For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily."

scripture.excerpt: For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
scripture.function: The definitive statement of Christ's complete deity — all, not part, of the Godhead; bodily, not abstractly.

scripture.excerpt: For it pleased the Father that in him should all fulness dwell.
scripture.function: God's sovereign intention: all fullness in Jesus — not distributed among divine persons.

scripture.excerpt: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles.
scripture.function: The mystery of godliness: God himself was manifest in human flesh — not merely sent a representative.

scripture.excerpt: God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself.
scripture.function: The Father was personally present in the man Christ — not directing from a distance.

scripture.excerpt: He that hath seen me hath seen the Father.
scripture.function: Jesus is not a window to the Father — he is the Father's personal, bodily disclosure.

scripture.excerpt: I and my Father are one.
scripture.function: Unity of identity, not merely of will — the Greek en (neuter) indicates oneness of essence.

scripture.excerpt: Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person.
scripture.function: The Son is the exact stamp of God's essential being — not a copy but the thing itself made visible.

scripture.excerpt: His name shall be called... The mighty God, The everlasting Father.
scripture.function: Isaiah names the Messiah with divine names belonging to YHWH — confirming full deity, not honorary titles.

vocabulary.definition: Greek word in Colossians 2:9 for "Godhead" or "Deity" — referring to the divine nature or essence in its fullness, not merely divine qualities.
vocabulary.relevance: The strongest possible Greek expression of full deity — not theiotes (divine quality) but theotes (the Deity itself).

vocabulary.definition: The Greek word in Col. 2:9 meaning "in bodily form" — referring to the physical incarnate humanity of Jesus as the permanent dwelling place of all divine fullness.
vocabulary.relevance: Establishes that the fullness of deity is not a metaphor but a permanent incarnational reality.

vocabulary.definition: 1 Timothy 3:16 — God appearing in human form; the incarnation as divine self- disclosure, not delegation.
vocabulary.relevance: The key phrase for understanding that the incarnation is God's own personal action, not the sending of a separate divine agent.

vocabulary.definition: The theological claim that Jesus is not partially divine or derivatively divine but
vocabulary.relevance: Distinguishes Oneness Christology from Arianism (derivative deity) and from

vocabulary.definition: Greek term in Hebrews 1:3 — the exact impression or stamp of something, like a seal on wax. Jesus is the exact impression of God's own being (hypostasis).
vocabulary.relevance: Establishes the ontological identity between Jesus and God — not resemblance but exact correspondence.

vocabulary.definition: The act by which God, in Christ, restored the broken relationship between humanity and himself — paying the debt of sin and removing the enmity.
vocabulary.relevance: The purpose clause of the incarnation — God became flesh in order to accomplish what only God could accomplish.

domains.title: Incarnation, Sonship, And The True Humanity Of Christ
domains.anchor: Galatians 4:4 — "But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law."

scripture.excerpt: The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee... therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God.
scripture.function: Son of God is an incarnational title — the angel grounds it in the virgin conception, not in eternal generation.

scripture.excerpt: God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law.
scripture.function: The Son came into existence through a woman — "made of a woman" is the origin of the Son.

scripture.excerpt: Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee.
scripture.function: Sonship is declared "this day" — a specific moment, not an eternal state without beginning.

scripture.excerpt: As the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same.
scripture.function: The Son genuinely shares human nature — not a phantom or semblance but real flesh and blood.

scripture.excerpt: He had to be made like his brothers in every way... to make atonement for the sins of the people.
scripture.function: True humanity is not incidental but necessary — atonement requires a genuine human mediator.

scripture.excerpt: The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.
scripture.function: The pre-existent Word (eternal) became flesh (incarnational) — two-stage Christology.

scripture.excerpt: Being in the form of God... he made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant.
scripture.function: The kenosis — God voluntarily accepted human limitations for the purpose of redemption.

scripture.excerpt: God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh.
scripture.function: God acted through the Son in genuinely human flesh — "likeness" means resemblance to, not identity with, sinful flesh.

vocabulary.definition: The act by which the eternal Word (God) took on human nature permanently in the person of Jesus — not a temporary appearance but a real assumption of humanity.
vocabulary.relevance: The central mystery of Christian theology — God truly became human without ceasing to be God.

vocabulary.definition: The title "Son of God" referring to the divine-human person born of Mary, conceived by the Holy Spirit — an incarnational designation, not an eternal pre-incarnation relationship.
vocabulary.relevance: Distinguishes Oneness Christology from trinitarian eternal generation; the Son has a beginning (Luke 1:35).

vocabulary.definition: John 1:1 — the eternal self-expression,
vocabulary.relevance: The eternal dimension of Christ: the Word

vocabulary.definition: Greek: "emptying" — Philippians 2:7 says Jesus "made himself of no reputation" (literally: emptied himself). He voluntarily accepted human limitations while retaining divine nature.
vocabulary.relevance: Explains how the fully divine Jesus could grow in wisdom (Luke 2:52), feel hunger, and not know the hour of his return (Mark 13:32).

vocabulary.definition: The theological affirmation that Jesus is simultaneously fully divine (the Spirit of the Father/Word) and fully human (the Son born of Mary) — neither nature abolished or confused.
vocabulary.relevance: The interpretive key for passages where Jesus appears limited (human nature speaking) or unlimited (divine nature acting).

vocabulary.definition: The trinitarian doctrine that the Son eternally proceeds from the Father within the Godhead — rejected by Oneness theology as unscriptural.
vocabulary.relevance: Understanding this rejected doctrine clarifies what Oneness theology affirms about sonship instead.

domains.title: Father, Son, And Holy Spirit In Scriptural Interpretation
domains.anchor: Matthew 28:19 — "...baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost."

scripture.excerpt: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name [singular] of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.
scripture.function: The great commission uses three titles but a single name — the name is Jesus (as Acts 2:38 and all baptismal records show).

scripture.excerpt: I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter... I will come to you.
scripture.function: Jesus promises the Comforter but then says "I will come to you" — the Comforter is the Spirit of the risen Jesus, not a third person.

scripture.excerpt: Why hath Satan filled thine heart to lie to the Holy Ghost?... thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God.
scripture.function: The Holy Spirit and God are identified — lying to the Spirit is lying to God.

scripture.excerpt: The Lord is that Spirit.
scripture.function: Paul explicitly identifies the Lord (Jesus) with the Spirit — not a conflation of persons but identification of the divine nature.

scripture.excerpt: I and my Father are one.
scripture.function: Jesus and the Father share one essence — the Greek neuter en ("one thing") indicates identity of nature, not merely agreement of will.

scripture.excerpt: Doubtless thou art our father... thou, O LORD, art our father, our redeemer; thy name is from everlasting.
scripture.function: The Father is identified with YHWH and the Redeemer — the Father title belongs to the one God, not a separate divine person.

scripture.excerpt: One Spirit... one Lord... one God and Father of all.
scripture.function: The three "ones" are not three persons of a Godhead — they are three aspects of one God viewed from different relational angles.

scripture.excerpt: God is a Spirit.
scripture.function: God's essential nature is Spirit — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are designations of the one Spirit who is God.

scripture.excerpt: The great commission's singular "name" (onoma) requires one name for three titles — the name is Jesus; Acts shows the apostles understood this and baptized accordingly.
scripture.function: The most important single grammatical observation in the baptism discussion.

vocabulary.definition: Three uses: (1) God as Father of all creation and Israel; (2) God as Father of Jesus — the divine Spirit that dwelt in the human Son; (3) God as Father of believers through adoption in Christ.
vocabulary.relevance: Distinguishes the three biblical uses of "Father" so students can read the texts accurately without importing a trinitarian person-to-person relationship.

vocabulary.definition: The incarnational title of the human nature of Jesus — the divine Spirit clothed in human flesh; the Father in flesh.
vocabulary.relevance: The Son is the visible, human dimension of the incarnate God — not a pre-incarnation eternal person.

vocabulary.definition: God in his active, operative presence — particularly the Spirit of God at work in the world and in believers; not a third person but God himself in active spiritual operation.
vocabulary.relevance: The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father (Matt. 10:20), the Spirit of Christ (Rom. 8:9), and the Spirit of Jesus (Acts 16:7) — consistently identified with the one God.

vocabulary.definition: Greek parakletos — one called alongside to help; used in John 14–16 for the Holy Spirit.
vocabulary.relevance: Jesus promises a Comforter (John 14:16) then says "I will come to you" (v.18) — the Comforter is the risen, spiritual presence of Jesus himself, not a third divine person.

vocabulary.definition: Theological term for the way God reveals himself through different roles and operations in the economy of redemption — Father (source/authority), Son (human manifestation), Spirit (indwelling presence).
vocabulary.relevance: Oneness theology affirms the economic distinctions without accepting the ontological trinity (three co-equal eternal persons).

domains.title: The Deity And Humanity Of Christ In Difficult Passages
domains.anchor: John 5:19 — "The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do: for what things soever he doeth, these also doeth the Son likewise."

scripture.excerpt: The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do.
scripture.function: Human dependence speaking — the incarnate Son operates through the Father's direction; not a second divine person receiving commands from the first.

scripture.excerpt: Of that day and that hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels which are in heaven, neither the Son, but the Father.
scripture.function: The Son (human nature) did not know; the Father (divine nature) knew — the dual nature resolves the apparent contradiction.

scripture.excerpt: Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man.
scripture.function: Genuine human development — the incarnate Jesus grew, which no eternal divine person can do.

scripture.excerpt: That they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.
scripture.function: Jesus speaking from his human perspective — "the only true God" refers to the divine nature (Father), distinguished from the human mission.

scripture.excerpt: O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.
scripture.function: The Gethsemane prayer — the human will of Jesus expressing genuine distress while submitting to the divine will.

scripture.excerpt: In all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.
scripture.function: Genuine human temptation — not simulation; required by the necessity of the incarnation for human redemption.

scripture.excerpt: God hath made that same Jesus... both Lord and Christ.
scripture.function: The exaltation declares what God has done through Jesus's human life, death, and resurrection — not a change in eternal status but a completion of the incarnational purpose.

scripture.excerpt: Then shall the Son also himself be subject unto him that put all things under him, that God may be all in all.
scripture.function: The eschatological subjection — at the end, the human-divine distinction of the incarnation is resolved as God becomes "all in all."

vocabulary.definition: 2nd-century writers (Justin Martyr, Athenagoras, Theophilus) who attempted to present Christianity to educated Greeks using Greek philosophical categories — including the Logos concept from Stoic/Platonic philosophy.

vocabulary.definition: The first ecumenical council, convened by Emperor Constantine, which produced the Nicene Creed affirming the Son as "of the same substance" (homoousios) as the Father — rejecting Arianism.
vocabulary.relevance: The political-theological event that codified the trinitarian framework as official imperial Christianity.

vocabulary.definition: The early Christian position (associated with Sabellius) that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three modes or manifestations of one God — close to Oneness theology but typically criticized for collapsing all historical distinctions.
vocabulary.relevance: Important to distinguish Oneness theology from classical modalism: Oneness affirms genuine incarnational distinction, not mere theatrical modes.
